vāseṭṭha.notes: The packet lacks an entry for Bhāradvāja’s fellow student in MN 98 and Snp 3.9. The pair are seeking ordination in DN 27. DN 13:13.1 addresses the student and names the ancient seer in the same sentence, so a single identification would mislabel one of them. The plural Vāseṭṭhā addresses the Mallas of Kusinārā in DN 16 and of Pāvā in DN 33. For the lay disciple, AN 6.119, AN 6.140 and AN 8.43 are adjacent citation hits. AN 8.43 addresses Visākhā.

vīra.notes: Thag 1.8:1.5 attributes the verse to Vīra Thera. The two Thig 1.7 hits refer to Vīrā Therī, the nun. DPD lists both names under the form vīrā.

yamaka.notes: AN 4.187 places Yamaka among King Eḷeyya’s men who honor Rāmaputta. SN 22.85:1.2 explicitly introduces a monk called Yamaka, for whom the packet supplies no entry.

yamataggi.notes: The same seer occurs between Vessāmitta and Aṅgīrasa as Yamataggi in MN 95:13.9, Yamadaggi in AN 5.192:3.1 and Yamadaggino in AN 7.52:9.3. DPD assigns the latter two forms to the separate headword yamadaggi, so those AN passages are missing from this mention list.

yamunā.notes: SN 13.3 and 13.4 both name the river at 1.3, with its English name one segment earlier. The same alignment hides mentions in SN 55.42 and SN 56.53–54. Thag 19.1:14.1 has yamunaṁ, translated at 14.2. The citation to SN 13.5 lands on the clay-ball simile. DN 20:11.5 calls the nāgas Yāmunā, those from the Yamunā.

yasa.notes: DN 20:13.4 names Yasa with Soma among the gods. The packet misses this mention because the dictionary gives yasasā only the common sense of fame. Thag 1.117:1.5 attributes the verse to Yasa Thera, for whom the packet supplies no entry.

yasavatī.notes: DN 14:1.12.7–8 names King Suppatita and Queen Vassavatī as Vessabhū’s parents. Both the Pāli and Sujato use Vassavatī for the mother whom DPD and DPPN call Yasavatī, explaining the empty mention list.

yugandhara.notes: DN 32:10.1 introduces the spirits and commanders to whom one can appeal. Yugandhara occurs in their list at 10.13. The packet has no entry for the mountain.

yāmā.notes: Sujato renders yāmā devā as ‘gods of Yama’ in MN 97:30.17–20. The English spelling accounts for the empty mention list. AN 3.70:31.1–4 gives their day and lifespan, AN 3.80:4.2 lists their realms, and Thig 8.1:2.1 names them in verse. AN 3.81 concerns the three trainings.

ñātika.notes: The brick house fixes the village’s identity across the spellings ñātike (SN 12.45) and nātike (DN 16, DN 18, MN 31, AN 6.19–20, AN 6.59, AN 8.73–74, AN 11.9 and SN 35.113). DPD puts nātike under nātika. The citation list also picks up neighbors AN 6.18, AN 8.72, AN 11.8, MN 30, SN 14.12, SN 35.112, SN 44.10 and SN 55.7. Check the entry’s account of Ambapālī’s gift. In DN 16 the Buddha has already left the village for Vesālī when she hosts him and gives the grove.

ākoṭaka.notes: SN 2.30:7.1–9.1 identifies the godling and Veṭambarī’s reply. The entry runs ‘Nigaṇṭha Makkhali’ together, but the verse enumerates the Jain ascetic and the bamboo-staffed ascetic separately. The neighboring SN 2.29 concerns Susīma.

ālakamandā.notes: The citation list omits DN 17. Its capital-city simile at 1.3.8 matches DN 16:5.18.5 and the entry’s second Dīgha page reference (DN.ii.170).

āmalakīvana.notes: MN 67:1.2 places the grove at Cātumā. The citation also reaches MN 66, which opens at Āpaṇa.
